MultipleChoice.prompt: This function opens an `AnyPool` so that a store can run on either SQLite or PostgreSQL, chosen by the connection URL. Calling it with a valid `sqlite::memory:` URL does not give a working pool. Which statement best identifies the bug in the marked line?
options: `install_default_drivers` only needs to run for PostgreSQL URLs, since SQLite support is built into `AnyPool`, so the line is harmless but redundant for this URL.
Calling `install_default_drivers` more than once per process is an error, so it must be removed from `open` and run from a `Once` guard.

The drivers are registered only after the pool has already tried to connect, so `connect` runs with no Any driver installed and fails (in current sqlx, it panics) before the registration line is reached.
`max_connections(5)` is invalid for an in-memory SQLite URL, because the Any driver cannot open more than one connection to SQLite.
reasons: No backend is built in automatically. The Any driver relies on registration for every backend, SQLite included, so skipping or delaying it breaks the SQLite URL too.
It is not the repeat call that is wrong here. The function is meant to be safe to call from a connect function, and the real problem is that the call comes too late.

The Any driver looks up the backend for the URL at connect time in a runtime registry. That registry is empty until `install_default_drivers` runs, so the call must come before any Any connection or pool is created.

The pool does not reject this setting. With `:memory:` several connections would each see their own empty database, which is a different problem. It is not what makes this code fail, and it is not tied to the registration line.

questions.explanation: The Any driver looks up the backend for the URL at connect time in a runtime registry. That registry is empty until `install_default_drivers` runs, so the call must come before any Any connection or pool is created.

MultipleChoice.prompt: An author replied with correct answers to the questions on head abc123. They then pushed head def456, and the Soqrates CI check ran. That run graded the earlier round, posted its results and posted new questions about one concept. Someone now clicks "Re-run" on the same CI check for head def456. What should happen, and why?
options: The re-run re-asks the earlier round's questions, because the author has not yet pushed a head that fixes the wrong answers.
The re-run grades the same answers again, so the author's history grows to 4 graded answers and the results comment is posted a second time, because each CI run is independent.

Nothing is graded or posted again. The first run claimed the pending session and kept a record that it was graded, so the re-run finds no ungraded session. The author's history keeps its 2 graded answers, and the check stays Pending for the new head's questions.
The re-run fails with an error because the answers were already consumed, and the author must push a new commit before the check can run again.
reasons: The earlier round has already been graded and its results posted. A re-run does not ask it again. It only concerns the questions for the current head, which were already posted and are not posted a second time.

This is the failure the design prevents. If grading were not once-only, each re-run or retry would add duplicate reviews and skew the author's spaced-repetition schedule. CI runs are not independent here, because the stored state carries over between them.

A session is graded at most once. The first run removes the pending session and stores a graded record, and applying that grading is idempotent. A re-run therefore has nothing left to grade and changes nothing. The review history is not duplicated.

The re-run does not fail. Re-running the check on the same head is a supported case, and it reports the existing state, still Pending for the new questions. Only submitting answers to an already-graded session is rejected, and the check run does not do that.

questions.explanation: A session is graded at most once. The first run removes the pending session and stores a graded record, and applying that grading is idempotent. A re-run therefore has nothing left to grade and changes nothing. The review history is not duplicated.

MultipleChoice.prompt: In this change the scanner keeps `open` as an optional pair of fence character and run length, instead of a simple in-code-block boolean. The closing arm requires the same character, a run at least as long as the opener, and nothing but whitespace after the run. What problem does this solve, and what would go wrong with a boolean that toggles on any line starting with three backticks?
options: A block opened with four backticks that shows a three-backtick example inside it would be closed early by the inner fence. The rest of the block would then be treated as ordinary text instead of code.
The check that nothing follows the run is there to strip trailing whitespace from the fence line so the code can print it cleanly.
Without the stored character and length, a tilde fence could never be opened, because the scanner would only recognise backticks.
The length is stored so that a closing fence must be exactly as long as the opener. A longer closing run is then rejected as malformed.
reasons: Storing the fence character and the run length lets the scanner ignore any line that is shorter than the opener or uses a different character. Only a line with the same character, at least as long as the opener and with nothing else after it, ends the block.
The check does not modify anything. It decides whether a line can close the block. A line such as three backticks followed by a language tag inside a block is content, so it must not close it.
The opening arm would still recognise both characters through the `fence` filter. The stored pair only matters for deciding what closes the block, not for what opens one.
CommonMark allows a closing run that is at least as long as the opener, and the code uses `run >= n`, not equality. A longer closing fence is valid and closes the block.

questions.explanation: Storing the fence character and the run length lets the scanner ignore any line that is shorter than the opener or uses a different character. Only a line with the same character, at least as long as the opener and with nothing else after it, ends the block.

MultipleChoice.prompt: Soqrates reads the answer field of question 1 from the comment body shown. The body is not wrapped in any other fence. Fenced blocks follow Markdown rules: a block opened with a run of tildes closes only on a line made of the same character, at least as long as the opener. Markers inside an open block are ignored. What does the parser read as the answer to question 1?execution

code.text:
~~~~
~~~
<!-- soqrates:answer=1 -->
decoy
<!-- soqrates:answer-end=1 -->
~~~
<!-- soqrates:answer=1 -->
real
<!-- soqrates:answer-end=1 -->

options: The answer for question 1 is "decoy", because the first complete field is the one that counts.
The answer for question 1 is "real", because the shorter tilde line closes the block and the second field is outside code.
No answer is read for question 1, because the four-tilde block is never closed by the shorter three-tilde lines and so swallows both fields.
Both fields are read and joined, giving "decoy" followed by "real".
reasons: The first field sits inside the open tilde block, where markers are ignored. The "first field counts" rule only applies to fields found outside code.
A closing fence must be at least as long as the opening one. The three-tilde lines are shorter than the four-tilde opener, so they do not close the block.

A tilde fence closes only on a tilde-only line with at least as many tildes as the opener. The three-tilde lines are too short, so the block stays open to the end of the comment. Both markers are treated as code, and question 1 has no field.
Fields are never joined. At most one field per question counts, and a field inside fenced code does not count at all.

questions.explanation: A tilde fence closes only on a tilde-only line with at least as many tildes as the opener. The three-tilde lines are too short, so the block stays open to the end of the comment. Both markers are treated as code, and question 1 has no field.

MultipleChoice.prompt: In this change the open-fence state went from just a run length to `Option<(char, usize)>`, and closing the block now needs the guard `fence == Some(c) && run >= n && trimmed[run..].trim().is_empty()`. What does this guard do that the old length-only state could not?
options: It guards against a panic. Without the character comparison, `trimmed[run..]` would index past the end of the string when the line is not a fence.

A closing line must use the same fence character as the opener, be at least as long, and have nothing after the run. Any other line inside the block falls through to the arm that keeps the state, so a `~~~` line inside a backtick block, or a shorter run inside a longer one, stays plain content.
It makes the scanner treat every line starting with a fence character as a new nested opener. The state is then replaced with the new character and length.
The guard is needed only because a pattern cannot be a tuple. Once `open` is destructured, the guard just unpacks `c` and `n`, and it does not change which lines close the block.
reasons: When the line is not a fence, `run` is 0 and `trimmed[0..]` is valid. The character comparison is about matching the opener's fence style, not about slice bounds.

The guard binds the opener's character and length from the `Some((c, n))` pattern and compares the current line against them. If it fails, the next arm, `Some(_)`, leaves `open` unchanged, so the block stays open.
Nothing nests here. While a block is open, the only transition is closing it, and only for a matching closer. Other fence-like lines are ignored, not stored as a new opener.
Tuple patterns work fine in `match`. The guard does real work: it decides whether this line is a valid closer. Without it, every line inside the block would match and close it.

questions.explanation: The guard binds the opener's character and length from the `Some((c, n))` pattern and compares the current line against them. If it fails, the next arm, `Some(_)`, leaves `open` unchanged, so the block stays open.
